bookJourney.chapters: The AI That Listens: Therapist, Companion, Secretary, and Cognitive Pimp
bookJourney.focus:
The AI That Listens: Therapist, Companion, Secretary, and Cognitive Pimp
Conversational AI entered mental health through a door the system had left open: lack of access. Therapists are too few, care is expensive, appointments are scarce, stigma persists, and crises do not respect office hours. A permanently available system that responds without sighing looks like the inevitable solution. It may indeed become part of the solution. This is precisely the moment to check where it keeps the knives.

beats.text: Psychological distress raises the book’s most uncomfortable commercial question.
Greater recognition and inadequate services can make a real need more visible.
Technology might reduce barriers while also creating new ways to monetize dependence.
The difference depends partly on what a company counts as success.
Longer use can mean value in one setting and unresolved vulnerability in another.
The book asks whether users can leave more autonomous than they arrived.
That question connects its market analysis to the ethics of product architecture.

beats.text: This is a book for readers willing to examine opportunity without sterilizing its human context.
Its distinctive perspective connects obvious demand with the vulnerability that gives demand its force.
The historical chapters explain how those needs change rather than simply disappear.
The market chapters offer signals, while the ethics chapters question what responding well would mean.
Begin with the prologue, then compare the Aspirin signal with the test of customer autonomy.
Follow the benefits, but also follow where the costs and dependencies land.
That is the reading invitation behind Aspirin, Viagra, and Coffins.
